choices: The office closes at five, please come early.
The office closes at five please come early.
The office closing at five. Please come early.
The office closes at five. Please come early.
answer: The office closes at five. Please come early.
hints: Each choice has two ideas: when the office closes, and a request. Look at how they are joined.
Two complete sentences cannot be joined by only a comma, or by nothing at all. That makes a run-on sentence.
Each part must be complete on its own, and two complete sentences must be separated by a period (or joined by a semicolon, or by a comma plus "and", "but" or "so"). Check each choice for both.

solution.methodName: Find the two complete thoughts, then check the join

steps.action: Find the two ideas: "The office closes at five" and "Please come early". Each is a complete sentence on its own.
steps.why: "Please come early" is a command, so its subject "you" is understood.

steps.action: The first choice joins two complete sentences with only a comma. This is a comma splice. Wrong.
steps.why: A run-on is two complete sentences joined without the right mark or joining word. A comma splice is a run-on that uses only a comma.

steps.action: The second choice has nothing between the two sentences. It is a run-on. Wrong.
The third choice starts with "The office closing at five." It has no full verb, so it is a fragment. Wrong.
The last choice separates two complete sentences with a period. Correct.
The answer is "The office closes at five. Please come early."

trapNotes.The office closes at five, please come e: A comma feels like the right pause in speech. But a comma alone cannot join two complete sentences. This is a comma splice.
trapNotes.The office closes at five please come ea: This is how we often say it out loud, in one breath. In writing, two complete sentences need a period between them.
trapNotes.The office closing at five. Please come: The period is in the right place, but "The office closing at five" has no full verb. It needs "closes".
